headline: Sunny, dry and milder-than-normal weather continues through Saturday, then a coastal storm is increasingly likely to bring wind and soaking rain to New York City and the surrounding area late Sunday into Monday, with the wettest computer models showing enough rain for flooding.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Thursday is clear and mostly sunny in New York City under strong high pressure, with highs in the upper 50s to mid 60s, several degrees above normal. Winds stay light, under about 10 mph, turning southwest this afternoon (possibly more southerly with a sea breeze), and a few thin high clouds drift in late. A weak disturbance passing overhead tonight into Friday morning stays dry, and with clear skies and calm air, patchy freezing fog is possible tonight in river valleys, sheltered inland spots and the Long Island Pine Barrens, bringing a low chance of black ice on bridges and overpasses.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Friday and Saturday stay mostly sunny and dry, with highs again in the upper 50s to mid 60s, several degrees above normal. Nights gradually turn a few to several degrees milder than normal into the weekend, especially in the city and right along the coast, though clear, calm nights through Saturday night will still let outlying areas cool off. As the air slowly gets more humid, overnight fog becomes more likely in outlying areas, particularly river valleys.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: A coastal storm is increasingly likely to affect the area late Sunday into Monday, with rain and lower clouds possible Sunday, rain likely early Monday, and improvement possible Monday afternoon; it could have some tropical or subtropical traits, so the National Hurricane Center is worth checking. The wettest computer models show a swath of up to about 4 inches of rain from the Mid-Atlantic to southern New England, and since about 3 inches in 6 hours is enough to cause flooding here, that could mean widespread minor flooding and isolated flash flooding in the most flood-prone spots; the European model remains an outlier against this wetter, single-storm scenario. Peak wind gusts are estimated at 30–40 mph, but could be higher if the storm deepens and tracks close to the coast, with northwest gusts around 25–30 mph Monday as it pulls away.

coast: Winds and seas stay below Small Craft Advisory levels through Saturday under high pressure. Winds and waves build Sunday into Monday as the coastal storm approaches, with ocean seas reaching 5 ft or more by late Sunday and gale-force winds possible on all waters Monday, depending on the storm's track and strength; the Monday gale potential has now been added to the Hazardous Weather Outlook. Higher-than-usual tides around Tuesday's full moon could bring minor coastal flooding depending on the storm's track and intensity, and one coastal flood model ensemble already hints at minor flooding Sunday night.
watch_for: The track and strength of the Sunday–Monday coastal storm, which will decide how much rain, wind and coastal flooding New York City gets.
Heavy rain of up to about 4 inches in the wettest scenarios, which could cause widespread minor flooding and isolated flash flooding.
Patchy freezing fog and a low chance of black ice on bridges and overpasses in valleys and sheltered inland areas tonight.
confidence: Forecasters are confident in dry, mild weather through Saturday, but the late Sunday–Monday storm remains a forecast challenge, with its track, timing, rain totals and winds still uncertain as computer models disagree.
